newsitem.title: USA: Minorities drop sharply in Calif. law school class.
newsitem.headline: Minorities drop sharply in Calif. law school class.

text.p: Only one black student was in the 270-member class that entered the University of California at Berkeley's law school Monday, the first new class since the university scrapped affirmative action.
The incoming class at Boalt Hall law school also reflected sharp drops in enrollment of most other minorities.
The University of California has been at the center of controversy since its governing Board of Regents voted in 1995 to scrap racial preferences in student admissions.
The new admissions policy is taking effect for the university's law schools and other graduate programs. For undergraduates, the new policy takes effect from the spring of next year.
The new policy was backed by California Gov. Pete Wilson but opposed by some students and academics in the sprawling nine-campus university system.

"Today, the Class of 2000 enters Boalt Hall. As a result of the regents' policy decisions ... this class has no native Americans, and fewer African-Americans, Chicanos and Latinos than any of our entering classes since the mid-1960s," the dean of Boalt Hall law school, Herma Hill Kay, said.
"Although we had anticipated that the race-neutral policy would produce a sharp drop in our minority students, we had not expected such dire results," she said in a statement.
This year, Boalt law school offered places to 15 black students, but none accepted. The only African-American in the incoming class accepted a place last year but delayed entry.
Last year, 20 of the 74 black students accepted decided to attend.
The lone black student, Eric Brooks, said he was "greatly surprised and disappointed" when he learned that he was the only black in the incoming class.

The new class includes seven Latino students, compared with 28 last year. Two native Americans were offered places in this year's class, but both decided to enroll elsewhere. Last year, there were four native Americans in the first-year class.
The number of Asian students accepted increased to 113 from 101 last year, but the number enrolled fell to 32 from 38.

Explaining why so few minority students accepted the places that were offered at Boalt Hall, UC Berkeley said that some students expressed concerns about coming to Boalt Hall in light of the change in policy.
Another important reason was that Boalt Hall did not provide the same level of financial support as other leading law schools, UC Berkeley said in a "question and answer" sheet on its Internet site.

The U.S. Department of Education said last month that it had launched a probe of whether the student admissions policies of Boalt and two other University of California law schools were racially discriminatory.
Jennifer Nelson, executive director of the American Civil Rights Institute, a non-profit group opposed to racial preferences, said racial preferences were "not the answer to achieving diversity."
"What we need to do is fix schools at the lower level, make sure all kids in the state are getting a really good education," she said.

Last November, Californians approved a statewide ballot measure abolishing affirmative action programs in state government. A federal appeals court upheld the law in April, but civil rights groups are appealing the ruling.
